1.content_html:
What Is Homeostasis?

Your body works best when its internal conditions stay within narrow limits. Homeostasis is the process that keeps factors such as body temperature, blood glucose concentration and water balance at optimal levels. Without homeostasis, enzymes would denature and chemical reactions inside cells would slow down or stop entirely.

Key Fact

Homeostasis maintains a stable internal environment by controlling conditions such as body temperature, blood glucose concentration and water balance — all of which affect enzyme activity.

All homeostatic control systems involve three key components. A receptor detects a change in the environment (a stimulus). A coordination centre (such as the brain or spinal cord) receives and processes the information. An effector (a muscle or gland) carries out the response to bring the condition back to its set point.

The Nervous System

The nervous system enables humans to react to their surroundings and coordinate behaviour. It uses electrical impulses that travel along nerve cells to produce fast, short-lived responses. The central nervous system (CNS) consists of the brain and the spinal cord. Information from receptors passes along sensory neurones to the CNS, which then sends signals along motor neurones to effectors.

There are three types of neurone you need to know. Sensory neurones carry impulses from receptors to the CNS. Relay neurones are found entirely within the CNS and connect sensory neurones to motor neurones. Motor neurones carry impulses from the CNS to effectors.

Each neurone has a cell body containing the nucleus, thin fibres called axons and dendrons. The axon is often surrounded by a myelin sheath — a fatty layer that insulates the nerve fibre and speeds up the transmission of impulses.

Synapses

Neurones do not touch each other directly. The tiny gap between two neurones is called a synapse. When an electrical impulse reaches the end of the first neurone, it triggers the release of chemical neurotransmitters. These chemicals diffuse across the synaptic gap and bind to receptors on the membrane of the next neurone, triggering a new electrical impulse. This means signals can only travel in one direction across a synapse.

Key Fact

At a synapse, electrical signals are converted into chemical signals (neurotransmitters) and then back into electrical signals in the next neurone. This ensures impulses travel in one direction only.

The Reflex Arc

A reflex action is an automatic, rapid response to a potentially harmful stimulus. Reflexes protect the body — for example, pulling your hand away from a hot object or your pupil constricting in bright light.

The pathway of a reflex is called a reflex arc. It follows this sequence:

Stimulus → Receptor → Sensory neurone → Relay neurone (in CNS) → Motor neurone → Effector → Response
1.exam_tip_html:
For example, if you touch a hot plate, pain receptors in your skin detect the stimulus. The impulse travels along a sensory neurone to a relay neurone in the spinal cord. The relay neurone passes the impulse to a motor neurone, which stimulates the effector (a muscle in your arm) to contract and pull your hand away. This all happens without conscious thought — your brain is not involved in the initial response.

Key Fact

The reflex arc follows the pathway: stimulus → receptor → sensory neurone → relay neurone (CNS) → motor neurone → effector → response. The brain is bypassed, making the response extremely fast.

Why Homeostasis Matters

The internal environment must stay stable because cells depend on enzyme-controlled reactions. Enzymes have an optimum temperature and pH — if conditions drift too far from the optimum, enzymes change shape (denature) and can no longer catalyse reactions. This is why the body constantly monitors and adjusts conditions using the receptor → coordination centre → effector pathway described above.

Both the nervous system and the endocrine (hormonal) system play roles in homeostasis. The nervous system produces fast, short-term responses via electrical impulses, while the endocrine system produces slower, longer-lasting responses via hormones. You will explore the endocrine system in the next lesson.

In extended-response questions on the nervous system, make sure you describe the full reflex arc pathway in the correct order. A common mistake is to say the brain controls reflex actions — it does not. State clearly that the relay neurone is in the spinal cord and that the response is automatic and involuntary. Use precise terminology: receptor, sensory neurone, relay neurone, motor neurone, effector.

4.content_html:
The Structure of DNA

DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) is a polymer found in the nucleus of cells. It is shaped as a double helix — two strands twisted around each other like a spiral ladder. Each strand is made up of repeating units called nucleotides.

Each nucleotide consists of three parts: a sugar (deoxyribose), a phosphate group and one of four bases — adenine (A), thymine (T), cytosine (C) or guanine (G). The two strands are linked by complementary base pairs joined by weak hydrogen bonds. Adenine always pairs with thymine (A–T), and cytosine always pairs with guanine (C–G).

Key Fact

A nucleotide = sugar + phosphate + base. The base pairing rules are: A pairs with T, and C pairs with G. The strands are held together by weak hydrogen bonds between complementary base pairs.

Genes, Genomes and Protein Synthesis

A gene is a section of DNA that codes for a specific protein. Different proteins control different characteristics. The genome is the entire DNA of an organism — all of its genes and the DNA between them. Understanding the genome helps scientists identify genes linked to diseases and develop new treatments.

Genes are found on chromosomes inside the nucleus. Humans have 23 pairs of chromosomes (46 in total). Each gene can exist in different versions called alleles, and it is the combination of alleles that determines an organism’s characteristics.

Meiosis is a type of cell division that produces sex cells (gametes) — sperm in males and eggs (ova) in females. Unlike mitosis, meiosis produces four daughter cells, each with half the number of chromosomes of the parent cell. These cells are haploid (23 chromosomes in humans).

Because meiosis involves shuffling of genetic material, each gamete is genetically different. When two gametes fuse at fertilisation, the resulting zygote has the full set of 46 chromosomes and a unique combination of alleles from both parents.

Monohybrid Inheritance

Inheritance describes how characteristics are passed from parents to offspring through alleles. An allele can be dominant (shown with a capital letter, e.g. B) or recessive (lowercase, e.g. b). A dominant allele is always expressed when present. A recessive allele is only expressed when two copies are inherited (one from each parent).

An organism with two identical alleles for a gene is homozygous (BB or bb). An organism with two different alleles is heterozygous (Bb). The combination of alleles is the genotype; the physical characteristic that is expressed is the phenotype.

Key Fact

Dominant alleles are expressed when one or two copies are present. Recessive alleles are only expressed when homozygous (two copies). Genotype = alleles an organism has. Phenotype = the characteristic shown.

A Punnett square is a diagram used to predict the possible outcomes of a genetic cross. You place the alleles from one parent along the top and the alleles from the other parent down the side. Each box shows a possible genotype of the offspring.
4.exam_tip_html:
For example, if both parents are heterozygous (Bb × Bb), the Punnett square gives: BB, Bb, Bb, bb. The ratio of phenotypes would be 3 dominant : 1 recessive. This means there is a 75% probability of the dominant phenotype and a 25% probability of the recessive phenotype.

You also need to understand how sex is determined. Females have two X chromosomes (XX), and males have one X and one Y (XY). A Punnett square for sex inheritance shows a 50:50 chance of the offspring being male or female.

Variation

Variation refers to the differences between individuals of the same species. Genetic variation is caused by differences in DNA — these arise through mutations and the mixing of alleles during sexual reproduction (meiosis). Environmental variation results from the conditions an organism lives in, such as diet, sunlight or exercise.

Most characteristics are influenced by both genes and the environment. Most phenotypic features result from multiple genes rather than a single gene. Mutations occur naturally and produce new alleles. Most mutations have no effect on the phenotype. Some have a small effect, and very rarely a single mutation can significantly change the phenotype.

Key Fact

Variation can be genetic (from DNA/alleles), environmental (from surroundings) or both. Most mutations have no effect on phenotype. Most phenotypic features are controlled by multiple genes.

The Human Genome Project

The Human Genome Project was a major international effort to map and sequence every gene in the human genome. Its potential applications include identifying genes linked to inherited diseases, developing personalised medicines, understanding evolutionary relationships between species and advancing forensic science.

When drawing a Punnett square, always show the parental genotypes, the gametes, and the offspring genotypes and phenotypes. State the ratio clearly (e.g. 3:1 or 1:1). A common error is to write the probability as a certainty — say “there is a 25% chance” rather than “one in four offspring will be”. Remember these are probabilities, not guarantees.
